title: Telling My Story
overview: Level 2 opens where most people are asked to speak first: an account of their own life. That is harder than it sounds, because a life is not a sequence of events but a set of turning points, and English marks the difference. This unit gives you the prepositions that follow adjectives, the form for habits that have stopped, and the time expressions that hold a long narrative together. It ends with two personal statements about the same life, one that works and one that does not.
learningPath: Read and listen to the Lesson. There are three patterns.
Open Patterns. Card 1 has no rule — it is a list, and it has to be learned as one.
Learn the words. Twenty-nine, in five groups.
Read the three texts aloud. The third is two personal statements about one life.
Do the Practice. Practice 3 is where a list becomes a narrative.
Record yourself telling four minutes of your own story.
Take the quiz, then update My progress.
lectureScript:
Welcome to Level 2. The English gets less mechanical from here, and this first unit sets the tone: there is one pattern with no rule at all, one small verb form, and one thing that is not grammar and matters more than either.
First, adjective plus preposition.
Good at. Interested in. Worried about. Keen on. Aware of. Capable of. Proud of. Disappointed with.
There is no rule. I want to be honest about that early, because you will look for one and there is not one to find. Why is it good at and not good in? No reason that helps you. The pairings are fixed by use, and they are learned as pairs, exactly like the irregular verbs in Level 1 Unit 14.
What I can give you is a small amount of order.
Of is the commonest by a distance — aware of, capable of, proud of, afraid of, tired of, fond of.
About tends to go with feelings pointed at a situation — worried about, excited about, annoyed about, sorry about.
With tends to go with feelings pointed at a person or a thing you have dealt with — pleased with, disappointed with, bored with, satisfied with.
At goes with ability — good at, bad at, brilliant at, hopeless at.
And in goes with attention — interested in, involved in, absorbed in.
Those tendencies cover perhaps two thirds of the common pairs and they will mislead you occasionally. Learn the pairs; use the tendencies to guess when you are stuck.
One thing that will save you errors: what follows the preposition is a noun or an -ing form, never a plain verb. Interested in working here. Good at explaining things. Not interested in to work.
Second pattern: used to.
This is for a past habit or a past state that is now over.
I used to work nights. She used to live abroad. I used to smoke.
Every one of those carries the same implication: and I do not now. That implication is not optional and it is the whole point of the form. If you say I used to work nights, your listener understands that you no longer do, without you saying so.
The form is fixed. Used to plus the plain verb, and it never changes for person. I used to, she used to, they used to.
And the negative and question use did, exactly as in Level 1 Unit 14 — and when did appears, used goes back to use.
Did you use to work nights? I didn't use to like it.
That is the one spelling error people make. With did, it is use to, with no d. You will hear no difference at all when it is spoken, and it matters in writing.
Now two things used to is not.
It is not the same as the past simple. I worked nights for two years is a fact about a period. I used to work nights says it was a habit and it has stopped. Both are correct and they say different things.
And it is completely different from to be used to, which means to be accustomed to something. I'm used to working nights means I have adapted, and I probably still do. Used to work — a stopped habit. Used to working — an adaptation. One is followed by a plain verb and one by -ing, and that is how you tell them apart in writing.
Third pattern, and this one is not really grammar.
A life story is not a list of events. If you tell somebody everything that happened in order, you have given them a timetable, and they will remember none of it.
What English narrative does instead is mark the turning points and compress everything between them.
The compression phrases: for the next few years, throughout that period, over the following decade. These cover long stretches in six words.
The turning point markers: then something changed, that was when, it was at that point that. These say the thing that follows matters.
And the looking-back markers: by then, looking back, at the time I thought. These let you comment on an earlier moment from where you are now, which is the thing that makes an account sound reflective rather than chronological.
The shape that works is: compress, mark, expand. Cover five years in a sentence, mark the turning point, then slow down and give detail on the thing that actually mattered.
Most people do the opposite. They give equal detail to everything, run out of time, and never reach the part they were trying to explain.
Go to Patterns.

words.meaning: Very interested or enthusiastic. Takes on for a thing, to for an action.
words.example: I was never very keen on nights.
practice: She is keen to start as soon as possible.
He is keen on the idea but not the timing.
I am not keen on the new arrangement.
They were keen for us to stay.
words.starter: I was never very keen on
words.tutor: Say keen on something and keen to do something. The preposition changes with what follows.

words.meaning: Knowing that something exists or is happening. Takes of.
words.example: I was not aware of the change until afterwards.
practice: She is very aware of how she sounds.
Are you aware of the deadline?
I became aware of it gradually.
He seemed unaware of the problem.
words.starter: I was not aware of the change until
words.tutor: Say aware of and unaware of. The prefix from Unit 8 works normally here.

words.meaning: Able to do something. Takes of plus -ing.
words.example: She is capable of far more than the job asks.
practice: I am capable of doing it alone.
He is a capable engineer.
Nobody thought I was capable of it.
The machine is capable of running all night.
words.starter: She is capable of far more than the job
words.tutor: Notice capable of is followed by -ing, never a plain verb. Say capable of doing.

words.meaning: Pleased about something you or someone close has done. Takes of.
words.example: I am proud of how quickly I adapted.
practice: She was proud of the work rather than the result.
There is nothing to be proud of.
He is proud of his family.
I am proud of having finished it.
words.starter: I am proud of how quickly I
words.tutor: Say proud of a thing and proud of doing something. Both take of.

words.meaning: Feeling bad about something you did. Takes of.
words.example: I am not ashamed of changing my mind.
practice: He was ashamed of how he had reacted.
There is nothing to be ashamed of.
She seemed ashamed of the mistake.
I was ashamed of not asking sooner.
words.starter: I am not ashamed of changing my
words.tutor: Say ashamed of doing something. Notice it takes -ing, like capable and proud.

words.meaning: Sad because something was not as good as hoped. Takes with, by or in.
words.example: I was disappointed with the answer.
practice: She was disappointed by the response.
I was disappointed in myself.
He was disappointed but not surprised.
They were disappointed with how it ended.
words.starter: I was disappointed with the
words.tutor: Say disappointed with a thing and disappointed in a person. The preposition shifts the meaning.

words.meaning: The period when you are a child.
words.example: My childhood was spent mostly outdoors.
practice: It was a happy childhood.
I remember very little of my early childhood.
That habit goes back to childhood.
She had an unsettled childhood.
words.starter: My childhood was spent mostly
words.tutor: Say one sentence about childhood using used to. It is the natural pairing.

words.meaning: The way you were raised, and its effect on you.
words.example: My upbringing made me cautious about money.
practice: It was a strict upbringing.
Our upbringings were very different.
That comes from my upbringing.
She credits her upbringing for it.
words.starter: My upbringing made me cautious about
words.tutor: Childhood is the period; upbringing is how you were raised. Say the difference.

words.meaning: All the people born at about the same time.
words.example: My generation grew up without any of this.
practice: It skipped a generation.
The older generation sees it differently.
Three generations lived in that house.
Each generation solves it again.
words.starter: My generation grew up without any of
words.tutor: Say what your generation grew up with or without. Use used to.

words.meaning: Your education, experience and family circumstances.
words.example: My background is in engineering rather than teaching.
practice: We come from similar backgrounds.
She has a background in law.
It is not relevant to my background.
Tell me about your background.
words.starter: My background is in engineering rather than
words.tutor: Notice background is in a field. Say your own background in one sentence.

words.meaning: An important event marking a stage.
words.example: Getting that first contract was a real milestone.
practice: It was an important milestone for us.
The next milestone is in June.
She passed the milestone without noticing.
There were three milestones that year.
words.starter: Getting that first contract was a real
words.tutor: Name one milestone in your own life, in one sentence.

words.meaning: The moment when a situation begins to change direction.
words.example: The turning point was when the factory closed.
practice: That was the turning point for me.
There was no single turning point.
Looking back, it was the turning point.
The real turning point came later.
words.starter: The turning point was when the factory
words.tutor: Say the turning point was when. It is the frame that marks the important part of a story.

words.meaning: Slowly, over a period of time.
words.example: Gradually it became normal.
practice: The work gradually got easier.
I gradually stopped noticing.
It changed gradually rather than suddenly.
Gradually I realised I was wrong.
words.starter: Gradually it became
words.tutor: Say gradually and suddenly from Level 1 in two sentences about the same change.

words.meaning: In the end, after a long time.
words.example: Eventually I stopped applying.
practice: It eventually worked.
Eventually somebody explained it.
We got there eventually.
Eventually the whole thing was cancelled.
words.starter: Eventually I stopped
words.tutor: Eventually implies a long wait. Say finally and eventually and notice the difference.

words.meaning: Before the time being talked about.
words.example: I had previously worked in a warehouse.
practice: Previously, nobody had asked.
As previously agreed.
She previously lived abroad.
It had previously been a shop.
words.starter: I had previously worked in a
words.tutor: Previously is more formal than before. Say where you would use each.

words.meaning: At the beginning, before things changed.
words.example: Originally I intended to stay a year.
practice: It was originally a school.
Originally there were four of us.
That was not the original plan.
Originally I was not keen on the idea.
words.starter: Originally I intended to stay a
words.tutor: Originally sets up a change. Say originally, then say what happened instead.

words.meaning: At the present time, compared with the past.
words.example: Nowadays I would answer differently.
practice: Nowadays everybody applies online.
It is much easier nowadays.
Nowadays I do not mind at all.
That does not happen nowadays.
words.starter: Nowadays I would answer
words.tutor: Nowadays pairs naturally with used to. Say I used to, but nowadays.

words.meaning: At the same time, in another part of the story.
words.example: Meanwhile, the situation at home had changed.
practice: Meanwhile nothing had been decided.
She was studying; meanwhile I was working.
Meanwhile, the deadline was getting closer.
Meanwhile, everybody else had left.
words.starter: Meanwhile, the situation at home had
words.tutor: Meanwhile moves the story to a second thread. Use it once in a narrative.

words.meaning: The effect somebody or something has on you.
words.example: The biggest influence was a teacher I had at fifteen.
practice: It had a strong influence on me.
She was a good influence.
The influence was indirect.
I was under the influence of that idea for years.
words.starter: The biggest influence was a teacher I had at
words.tutor: Notice an influence on somebody. Name one influence in your own life.

words.meaning: A chance to do something.
words.example: The opportunity came from somebody I hardly knew.
practice: I did not take the opportunity.
It was an opportunity to start again.
There were few opportunities then.
The opportunity closed very quickly.
words.starter: The opportunity came from somebody I hardly
words.tutor: Say an opportunity to do something. It takes to plus a plain verb.

words.meaning: A fact or condition affecting a situation.
words.example: The circumstances were not in my control.
practice: In the circumstances, it was the right decision.
Circumstances changed halfway through.
It depends on the circumstances.
Under no circumstances would I do it again.
words.starter: The circumstances were not in my
words.tutor: Say in the circumstances. It is a useful phrase for explaining a decision.

words.meaning: Something difficult that tests you.
words.example: The real challenge was not the work.
practice: It was a challenge from the start.
I enjoy a challenge.
The biggest challenge was the language.
That was the hardest challenge of the year.
words.starter: The real challenge was not the
words.tutor: Say what the real challenge was in something you did. Often it is not the obvious thing.

words.meaning: Something you have done successfully.
words.example: The achievement I am proudest of is quite small.
practice: It was a real achievement.
She listed three achievements.
That is no small achievement.
The achievement was finishing at all.
words.starter: The achievement I am proudest of is quite
words.tutor: Say one achievement using proud of. The two go together naturally.

words.meaning: Sadness about something you did or did not do.
words.example: My one regret is not asking sooner.
practice: I have no regrets about it.
It is my only regret.
She said it with real regret.
Regret is not the same as shame.
words.starter: My one regret is not asking
words.tutor: Notice regret takes -ing for something you did: regret not asking.

words.meaning: To remember something, often with effort.
words.example: I recall it differently now.
practice: As far as I recall, it was March.
I cannot recall exactly what was said.
She recalled the whole conversation.
I recall being surprised.
words.starter: I recall it differently
words.tutor: Say as far as I recall. It is a useful hedge when you are not certain.

words.meaning: To think carefully about something in the past.
words.example: Reflecting on it now, I would decide the same way.
practice: I have reflected on it a lot.
She reflected before answering.
Looking back and reflecting are not the same.
It took a year to reflect properly.
words.starter: Reflecting on it now, I would decide the same
words.tutor: Say reflecting on it now. It signals a comment from the present about the past.

words.meaning: To agree that something is true, often unwillingly.
words.example: I have to admit I was wrong about that.
practice: She admitted it straight away.
I admit I was not keen at first.
He would not admit the mistake.
I must admit it worked.
words.starter: I have to admit I was wrong about
words.tutor: Notice admit takes -ing: admit being wrong, or a whole clause. Say both.

words.meaning: To become aware of something you had not understood.
words.example: It was years before I realised why.
practice: I realised too late.
She realised what was happening.
I did not realise it mattered.
Only afterwards did I realise.
words.starter: It was years before I realised
words.tutor: Say I did not realise. It is one of the most common openings for an explanation.

words.meaning: To recognise the value of something, or to be grateful.
words.example: I appreciate now what that cost her.
practice: I appreciate your help.
I did not appreciate it at the time.
She appreciates directness.
You have to appreciate how difficult it was.
words.starter: I appreciate now what that cost
words.tutor: Say I did not appreciate it at the time. It is a looking-back sentence.

readings.title: The Prepositions Have No Rule
readings.passage:
Good at. Interested in. Worried about. Pleased with. Capable of.
There is no rule behind those, and it is worth being told plainly, because you will spend time looking for one otherwise. Why at for ability and in for attention? There is a history, and it will not help you produce the right word in conversation.
They are learned as pairs, like the irregular verbs — the adjective and its preposition as one item, not two.
What can be offered is a set of tendencies. They are not rules and they will fail sometimes, but they cover a useful proportion of the common pairs.
Of is the most frequent by a wide margin. Aware of, capable of, proud of, afraid of, tired of, fond of, ashamed of. If you are stuck and must guess, of is the best guess.
About attaches to feelings pointed at a situation. Worried about, excited about, annoyed about, sorry about.
With attaches to feelings pointed at a person or something you have dealt with. Pleased with, disappointed with, bored with, satisfied with.
At attaches to ability. Good at, bad at, hopeless at, brilliant at.
In attaches to attention. Interested in, involved in, absorbed in.
One structural point that prevents more errors than all the tendencies together. Whatever follows the preposition is a noun or an -ing form. Never a plain verb.
Interested in working here. Capable of doing it. Proud of having finished.
Not interested in to work, not capable of do it.
That rule has no exceptions, which makes it the most valuable thing on this page.

readings.title: A Life Is Not a Timetable
readings.passage:
Ask somebody to tell you about their life and most people begin at the beginning and proceed at a constant speed. They give the same amount of detail to a school they attended for two years and to the decision that changed everything, and they run out of time before reaching the part they were actually trying to explain.
English narrative does something different, and it is a structural habit rather than a grammatical one.
It compresses, marks, and expands.
Compression covers long periods in very few words. For the next few years, not much changed. Throughout that period I was doing the same work. Over the following decade the industry shrank. Six or eight words can carry a decade, and doing so is not a failure to give detail — it is a signal that nothing there needs any.
Marking says the next thing matters. Then something changed. That was when I decided. It was at that point that the whole thing became impossible. These sentences are short and they exist to make the listener pay attention.
Expansion is where the detail goes, and it goes only after a mark.
There is a fourth move that separates a good account from a merely organised one: looking back. By then I had stopped expecting anything. At the time I thought it was a setback. Looking back, it was the best thing that could have happened.
Those sentences comment on a past moment from where you stand now, and they are what make an account sound reflective rather than chronological. They also do something practical — they tell the listener what to make of an event, so they are not left guessing whether it was good news.
A useful discipline: whatever length you have, spend half of it on one thing. If you have four minutes, three minutes of it should cover a period of weeks.

readings.title: The Same Life, Written Twice
readings.setting: Two versions of a personal statement for the same course application.
readings.passage:
VERSION A

  I was born in 1994. I went to primary
  school and then to secondary school. I
  left school at eighteen. I worked in a
  shop for one year. Then I worked in a
  warehouse for three years. Then I worked
  in an office for two years. In 2021 I
  moved. I worked in another warehouse for
  two years. Now I want to study.

  I am interested in this course. I am
  good at working hard. I am capable of
  learning new things. I am keen to start.

-----------------------------------------

  VERSION B

  For the first eight years after school I
  did warehouse and shop work, and none of
  it was chosen - it was what was
  available.

  The turning point was small. In 2019 my
  supervisor asked me to work out why one
  delivery route was always late. It took
  me three weeks. I found that two drivers
  were being given overlapping schedules
  by two different systems that had never
  been reconciled.

  Nobody had asked the question before,
  and I had not known I would enjoy it. I
  spent the following two years quietly
  redesigning things nobody had asked me
  to redesign.

  At the time I thought I was avoiding my
  actual job. Looking back, it was the
  only part of it I was any good at.

  I am applying because I would rather do
  that deliberately than by accident. I am
  aware I have no formal background in it,
  and I am capable of catching up.

comprehension.q: Why does the text say plainly that there is no rule?
comprehension.a: Because you will spend time looking for one otherwise, and the history behind the pairings will not help you produce the right word in conversation.
comprehension.why: Telling a learner that a system is arbitrary is more useful than letting them search for a pattern that does not exist.

comprehension.q: Which preposition is the best guess if you are stuck, and why?
comprehension.a: Of — it is the most frequent by a wide margin.
comprehension.why: A guessing strategy is worth having for the moment in conversation when the pair does not arrive.

comprehension.q: What structural point does the text call the most valuable on the page?
comprehension.a: Whatever follows the preposition is a noun or an -ing form, never a plain verb.
comprehension.why: It is the only thing in the pattern with no exceptions, which makes it more reliable than any of the tendencies.

comprehension.q: What are the three moves of English narrative?
comprehension.a: Compress a long period, mark the turning point, then expand on what mattered.
comprehension.why: The structure is the content here. Learners who organise chronologically produce a timetable rather than a story.

comprehension.q: Why does the text say compression is not a failure to give detail?
comprehension.a: Because covering a decade in eight words is a signal that nothing in it needs any detail.
comprehension.why: Compression communicates something. Learners often feel that skipping years is dishonest, and it is the opposite — it directs attention.

comprehension.q: What does the fourth move, looking back, do that the other three do not?
comprehension.a: It comments on a past moment from where you stand now, which makes an account sound reflective, and it tells the listener what to make of an event.
comprehension.why: Without it, the listener has to guess whether an event was good or bad news. The looking-back sentence removes the guess.

comprehension.q: Version A covers the same years as Version B. What is wrong with it?
comprehension.a: It is a timetable. Every period gets the same weight, nothing is marked as important, and the reader learns no more from the eighth sentence than from the first.
comprehension.why: Nothing in Version A is inaccurate or ungrammatical, which is exactly the point — it fails on structure alone.

comprehension.q: Version B compresses eight years into one sentence. What does that sentence achieve?
comprehension.a: It covers the period and characterises it — none of it was chosen, it was what was available — so the reader knows both what happened and what it meant.
comprehension.why: One sentence does two jobs. Version A takes six sentences to do the first job and never does the second.

comprehension.q: Both versions use adjective and preposition pairs. Why do B's work better?
comprehension.a: A's are unattached — good at working hard, capable of learning — and could describe anybody. B's are attached to evidence: aware I have no formal background, capable of catching up, said after three paragraphs that demonstrate it.
comprehension.why: The grammar is identical in both. What differs is whether the claim has anything behind it, which is a writing decision rather than a language one.

comprehension.q: Version B ends with two sentences using at the time and looking back. What do they do?
comprehension.a: They reinterpret the whole story — the thing the writer thought was avoidance turns out to be the point — and they tell the reader how to read everything above.
comprehension.why: This is the looking-back move doing the heaviest possible work. Placed at the end, it recasts three paragraphs the reader has already accepted.

grammar.title: Adjective + preposition
grammar.explanation: There is no rule. These are learned as pairs, like irregular verbs. What follows is a set of tendencies for guessing, and one structural point that never fails.
grammar.rule:
LEARN THE PAIR, NOT THE WORDS

TENDENCIES (not rules - they will fail)

  OF     the commonest by far. Best guess.
     aware of, capable of, proud of,
     afraid of, tired of, ashamed of

  ABOUT  feelings about a SITUATION
     worried about, excited about,
     annoyed about, sorry about

  WITH   feelings about a PERSON or
         something you've dealt with
     pleased with, disappointed with,
     bored with, satisfied with

  AT     ability
     good at, bad at, hopeless at

  IN     attention
     interested in, involved in

THE ONE RULE WITH NO EXCEPTIONS:
  what follows is a NOUN or an -ING form.
  NEVER a plain verb.

     interested in working here
     capable of doing it
     proud of having finished

     NOT  interested in to work
     NOT  capable of do it
grammar.workedExample:
You want to say that you would like to work somewhere.
1. Choose the adjective: interested.
2. Which preposition? Interested is about attention, so in. If you did not know, of would have been the best guess, and it would have been wrong — the tendencies help and do not guarantee.
3. Now the structural rule. What follows is a noun or an -ing form, never a plain verb.
4. To work is a plain verb with to. Change it to working.
5. Result: I am interested in working here.
Now one where the tendency helps. You want to say somebody can do more than the job requires.
1. Adjective: capable.
2. Guess of, which is the commonest — correct.
3. Apply the structural rule: capable of doing, not capable of do.
Result: She is capable of doing far more.
grammar.mistake: Putting a plain verb after the preposition — interested in to work, capable of do it. This is the most common error and the one rule that never fails, so it is worth fixing first. The other error is assuming a tendency is a rule: good in rather than good at, worried of rather than worried about. The tendencies are for guessing under pressure, not for construction.
grammar.tip: Learn the pair. After the preposition, a noun or -ing — never a plain verb.
grammar.practice:
Write the preposition and the correct form of the verb in brackets.
1. I am interested ____ (work) here.
2. She is capable ____ (do) far more.
3. I was worried ____ the delay.
4. He is good ____ (explain) things.
5. I am proud ____ (finish) it.
6. She was disappointed ____ the answer.
7. I am not keen ____ the new arrangement.
8. I was not aware ____ the change.
grammar.answers:
1. in working  2. of doing  3. about  4. at explaining  5. of finishing (or: of having finished)  6. with  7. on  8. of
Every verb became an -ing form. If any of yours is a plain verb or has to in front of it, that is the one rule with no exceptions and it is worth drilling until it is automatic.
Number 7 is the one the tendencies do not cover — keen takes on for a thing and to for an action, and it simply has to be learned.

grammar.title: Used to
grammar.explanation: For a past habit or state that is now over. The implication that it has stopped is not optional — it is the whole point of the form.
grammar.rule:
USED TO + PLAIN VERB
  I used to work nights.
  She used to live abroad.
  Never changes for person.

THE IMPLICATION IS ALWAYS:
  "...and I don't now."
  You don't have to say it. It is heard.

QUESTION AND NEGATIVE take did -
  and USED goes back to USE:
     Did you use to work nights?
     I didn't use to like it.
  ^ no d. You hear no difference.
    It matters in writing.

NOT THE SAME AS THE PAST SIMPLE:
  I worked nights for two years.
     a fact about a period
  I used to work nights.
     a habit, and it has stopped

COMPLETELY DIFFERENT FROM BE USED TO:
  I'm used to working nights.
     = I have adapted. I probably still do.

  used to WORK    a stopped habit
  used to WORKING an adaptation
grammar.workedExample:
You worked nights for several years and no longer do.
1. Is it a habit that has stopped? Yes. That is what used to is for.
2. Build it: used to plus the plain verb. I used to work nights.
3. Check what your listener now understands: that you do not work nights any more. You did not say it, and it was communicated.
Now the negative.
1. Negatives take did, exactly as in Level 1 Unit 14.
2. When did appears, used loses its d: I didn't use to work nights.
3. Say it aloud — it sounds identical. Write it and it does not.
And the one to keep separate: I'm used to working nights means I have adapted to them, and probably still do them. Plain verb after used to is a stopped habit. An -ing form after used to is an adaptation.
grammar.mistake: Writing didn't used to. In speech there is no difference at all, which is why the error survives; in writing it is visible. The other confusion is with be used to — I used to work nights and I'm used to working nights describe opposite situations, and the only signal is the form of the verb after to.
grammar.tip: Used to + plain verb means it stopped. Used to + -ing means you adapted.
grammar.practice:
Write the sentence.
1. You worked nights and no longer do.
2. She lived abroad and no longer does.
3. Ask somebody whether they worked nights in the past.
4. Say you did not like it at first, in the past.
5. Say you have adapted to working nights.
6. State a plain fact: you worked nights for two years.
grammar.answers:
1. I used to work nights.
2. She used to live abroad.
3. Did you use to work nights?
4. I didn't use to like it.
5. I am used to working nights.
6. I worked nights for two years.
Check 3 and 4 carefully: both have did, so both take use with no d.
Numbers 5 and 6 are the two that are not used to at all. Number 5 is be used to plus -ing — an adaptation. Number 6 is the past simple — a fact about a period, with no implication that anything stopped or continued.

grammar.title: Ordering a life story
grammar.explanation: Not grammar. A structural habit that decides whether an account communicates. English narrative compresses long periods, marks turning points, and expands only after a mark.
grammar.rule:
COMPRESS - cover years in a few words
  For the next few years, not much changed.
  Throughout that period I did the same work.
  Over the following decade the industry shrank.

MARK - say that the next thing matters
  Then something changed.
  That was when I decided.
  It was at that point that everything shifted.

EXPAND - detail goes here, and only here.

LOOK BACK - comment from now on then
  By then I had stopped expecting anything.
  At the time I thought it was a setback.
  Looking back, it was the best thing that
     could have happened.

THE SHAPE:  compress -> mark -> expand
THE TEST:   spend HALF your time on ONE thing.
            Four minutes? Three of them on
            a period of weeks.

WHAT MOST PEOPLE DO:
  equal detail everywhere, run out of time,
  never reach the point.
grammar.workedExample:
You have four minutes to explain how you ended up applying for something.
1. Compress everything before the turning point. For the first eight years after school I did warehouse and shop work, and none of it was chosen. One sentence, eight years.
2. Mark. The turning point was small. Short sentence, and it tells the listener to pay attention.
3. Expand. Now spend the bulk of your time here — what the task was, how long it took, what you found, why it mattered. This is three of your four minutes and it covers three weeks.
4. Look back. At the time I thought I was avoiding my actual job. Looking back, it was the only part of it I was any good at.
That last move does something the other three cannot: it tells the listener how to interpret everything above it, and it is placed last so it recasts what they have already accepted.
Compare the version that fails: eight sentences, one per job, equal length, no mark anywhere, and the listener has no idea which one you are building towards.
grammar.mistake: Giving equal detail to everything, which produces a timetable. The listener cannot tell what matters, and you run out of time before the part you were trying to explain. The other error is marking nothing — a story with no turning point sentence is a list, however interesting each item is.
grammar.tip: Compress, mark, expand. Half your time on one thing.
grammar.practice:
Write one sentence of each kind about your own life.
1. A compression covering at least three years.
2. A mark introducing a turning point.
3. An opening sentence of an expansion.
4. A looking-back sentence about how you saw it at the time.
5. A looking-back sentence about how you see it now.
6. Now put all five in order and read them aloud.
grammar.answers:
Model answers — yours will differ, and should.
1. For the next four years nothing much changed; I was doing the same work in three different places.
2. Then something happened that I did not think was important at the time.
3. I was asked to cover a colleague for two weeks, and the work turned out to be completely different from mine.
4. At the time I thought it was an interruption.
5. Looking back, those two weeks decided the next ten years.
Check yours against two things. Is the compression genuinely short — one sentence for at least three years? And do 4 and 5 disagree with each other? They should. If your at-the-time view and your looking-back view are the same, the sentence is doing no work.

speaking.title: Speaking 1 — Sixteen pairs
speaking.instructions:
Say sixteen adjective-and-preposition pairs aloud, each inside a true sentence about yourself.
Use at least three with of, three with about, three with with, two with at and two with in.
Record them.
Play back and check every one that is followed by a verb has the -ing form. That is the rule with no exceptions and it is the one to fix first.
speaking.tutor: Say twelve sentences with adjective and preposition pairs and ask the tutor to flag any wrong preposition.

speaking.title: Speaking 2 — Used to, three ways
speaking.instructions:
Take six things that were once true of you and are not now.
Say each one three ways: the statement, the question, the negative.
I used to work nights. Did you use to work nights? I didn't use to work nights.
Record all eighteen.
Then say two more sentences: one with be used to plus -ing, and one plain past simple about the same activity. Say aloud what is different about each.
speaking.tutor: Say six used-to sentences and ask the tutor what it now assumes about your present situation.

speaking.title: Speaking 3 — Compress a decade
speaking.instructions:
Take a period of at least five years in your own life.
Cover it in one sentence. Then in two. Then in one again, but a different one.
Do this for three different periods.
Record all nine sentences.
The hard part is that a compression should also characterise the period, not just cover it. Not I worked in three places, but none of it was chosen — it was what was available. Check each of yours does both.
speaking.tutor: Compress a period of your life into one sentence and ask the tutor what it now knows about that time.

speaking.title: Speaking 4 — Four minutes of your own story
speaking.instructions:
Tell four minutes of your own story, aimed at explaining how you arrived where you are now.
Use the shape: compress, mark, expand, look back.
Spend at least half the time on one thing.
Use at least four adjective-and-preposition pairs and at least two used-to sentences.
Record it.
Then listen twice, as in Level 1 Unit 19. On the second listening, time the expansion. If it is under half the total, the account is still a timetable.
speaking.tutor: Tell the tutor your four minutes and ask which part it thinks you were building towards.

speaking.title: Speaking 5 — At the time, and looking back
speaking.instructions:
Take five events from your own past.
For each, say two sentences: what you thought at the time, and what you think looking back.
At the time I thought it was a setback. Looking back, it was the best thing that could have happened.
Record all ten.
Check each pair disagrees. If the two halves say the same thing, the second sentence is doing no work, and this is the move that makes an account sound reflective rather than chronological.
speaking.tutor: Give the tutor five at-the-time sentences and ask it to guess how you see each one now.

speaking.title: Speaking 6 — Read both statements aloud
speaking.instructions:
Open Reading 3.
Read Version A aloud, then Version B.
Notice that Version A is entirely correct English.
Then say aloud: what is wrong with Version A, given that nothing in it is inaccurate or ungrammatical.
Then say what B's first sentence achieves that A's first six do not.
Then say what the last two sentences of B do to everything above them.
Record the last three parts and keep them.
speaking.tutor: Read the tutor Version A and ask what it still does not know about the writer.

writing.title: Writing 1 — Your story in four paragraphs
writing.prompt:
Write your own story in four paragraphs, following the shape.
Paragraph 1: compress everything before the turning point. No more than three sentences, covering at least three years.
Paragraph 2: mark the turning point. Two sentences at most.
Paragraph 3: expand. This must be the longest paragraph by a clear margin.
Paragraph 4: look back — what you thought at the time, and what you think now.
Use at least four adjective-and-preposition pairs and at least two used-to sentences.
writing.model:
For the first six years after I arrived I did whatever work was available — a shop, then two warehouses, then a shop again. I was not keen on any of it and I was not particularly good at it either. I used to tell people it was temporary.
Then something changed, and it was extremely small. A supervisor asked me to find out why one delivery route was always late.
It took three weeks. I was not aware at the start that anybody had ever asked the question, and it turned out nobody had. Two systems were producing schedules for the same drivers and neither knew about the other. I spent evenings on it because I was interested in it, which had not happened with any work before. When I explained it, the supervisor was surprised — not at the answer, but that I had kept going for three weeks without being asked to. I spent the next two years quietly doing more of that, mostly without permission.
At the time I thought I was avoiding my actual job, and I was slightly ashamed of it. Looking back, it was the only part of the job I was any good at, and I am proud of having noticed before somebody had to tell me.
writing.criteria: Paragraph 1 no more than three sentences covering at least three years; paragraph 2 no more than two sentences and clearly marking a change; paragraph 3 the longest by a clear margin; paragraph 4 contains an at-the-time view and a looking-back view that disagree; at least four adjective-and-preposition pairs; at least two used-to sentences
writing.support: Write paragraph 3 first and write it long. Then write paragraph 1 and force it under three sentences. Doing it in that order stops you spending your energy on the years that do not matter.
writing.extension: Count the words in paragraph 1 and paragraph 3. If 3 is not at least twice 1, the balance is still wrong.

writing.title: Writing 2 — Rewrite Version A
writing.prompt:
Use Version A in Reading 3.
Rewrite it so that it communicates, without inventing any facts that contradict it.
You may add detail of the kind Version B adds, but every date and job in A must still be accounted for — compressed, not deleted.
Then write four lines: what you compressed, what you marked, what you expanded, and what your looking-back sentence does.
writing.model:
For the eight years after I left school I moved between shop and warehouse work — a year in a shop, three in a warehouse, two in an office, then two more in a warehouse after I moved in 2021. None of it was a choice; it was what there was.
What changed was not a job. It was noticing, somewhere in the middle of the office years, that the part of the week I looked forward to was the part nobody had assigned me.
I had started fixing the stock spreadsheet because it was wrong and it annoyed me. Within a few months people were sending me things to check. Nobody arranged this and it was not part of my role. I was quite aware that it was not what I was being paid for, and I kept doing it because I was interested in it in a way I had never been interested in the actual job.
At the time I thought of it as a distraction from work I was not enjoying. Looking back, it was the only evidence I have that I would be any good at this, and it is why I am applying.

1. Compressed: all eight years and five jobs into one sentence, keeping every date.
2. Marked: what changed was not a job — a short sentence that refuses the expected kind of turning point.
3. Expanded: the spreadsheet, which took a few months and gets a whole paragraph.
4. The looking-back sentence turns a distraction into evidence, and it is what makes the application make sense.
writing.length: Four paragraphs plus four lines of commentary
writing.criteria: Every date and job from Version A still present; the compression covers at least six years in one or two sentences; a clear mark; an expansion that is the longest section; a looking-back sentence that reinterprets; four commentary lines
writing.support: List A's facts on one line first — 1994, school to 18, shop 1yr, warehouse 3yr, office 2yr, moved 2021, warehouse 2yr. Everything on that line must appear somewhere in your version, and most of it should appear in the first two sentences.
writing.extension: Give both versions to somebody who has read neither and ask what the person is like. Only one version answers that.

writing.title: Writing 3 — Read the two statements
writing.prompt:
Use the two personal statements in Reading 3. Write full-sentence answers.
1. Version A is entirely correct English. What is wrong with it?
2. What does B's first sentence achieve that A's first six do not?
3. Both versions use adjective and preposition pairs. Why do B's work better?
4. What do B's last two sentences do to everything above them?
5. Version B admits a weakness. Why does that strengthen rather than weaken it?
writing.model:
1. It is a timetable. Every period gets equal weight, nothing is marked as important, and the reader learns no more from the eighth sentence than from the first. The failure is structural, not linguistic.
2. It covers the same eight years and also characterises them — none of it was chosen, it was what was available. A's six sentences do the first job and never do the second.
3. A's are unattached and could describe anybody: good at working hard, capable of learning new things. B's are attached to three paragraphs of evidence, so capable of catching up is a conclusion the reader has already been given grounds for.
4. They reinterpret it. What the writer presents for three paragraphs as avoiding their actual job is recast as the only part they were good at, so the reader has to re-read everything above in a new light.
5. Because it is specific and it is immediately answered — I have no formal background in it, and I am capable of catching up. An admitted and addressed weakness reads as self-knowledge; an unmentioned one reads as either ignorance or concealment once the reader notices it.
writing.criteria: Five answers, each a full sentence; answer 1 identifies the failure as structural rather than linguistic; answer 3 contrasts attached and unattached claims; answer 4 uses the word reinterpret or an equivalent; answer 5 explains why the admission works
writing.support: Count the sentences in each version and count how many facts each contains. A has more sentences and fewer facts, and noticing that is most of the answer to question 1.
writing.extension: Write the one sentence you would add to Version A to improve it most, and say why that one.

writing.title: Writing 4 — Correct the ten mistakes
writing.prompt:
Every sentence has exactly one mistake from this unit.
Write each out correctly and say which pattern it came from.
1. I am interested in to work here.
2. She is capable of do far more.
3. I was worried of the delay.
4. He is good in explaining things.
5. I didn't used to like it.
6. Did you used to work nights?
7. I am used to work nights. (you have adapted and still do them)
8. I used to working nights. (a habit that stopped)
9. I worked in a shop. Then I worked in a warehouse. Then I worked in an office. (this is your whole first paragraph)
10. At the time I thought it was a mistake. Looking back, it was a mistake.
writing.model:
1. I am interested in working here. (Pattern 1 — a noun or -ing form after the preposition, never a plain verb)
2. She is capable of doing far more. (Pattern 1 — same rule)
3. I was worried about the delay. (Pattern 1 — about goes with feelings pointed at a situation)
4. He is good at explaining things. (Pattern 1 — at goes with ability)
5. I didn't use to like it. (Pattern 2 — with did, used loses its d)
6. Did you use to work nights? (Pattern 2 — same rule in the question)
7. I am used to working nights. (Pattern 2 — be used to takes -ing)
8. I used to work nights. (Pattern 2 — a stopped habit takes the plain verb)
9. For the next few years I moved between shop, warehouse and office work, and none of it was chosen. (Pattern 3 — compress, do not list)
10. At the time I thought it was a mistake. Looking back, it was the best decision I made that year. (Pattern 3 — the two halves must disagree, or the second does no work)
writing.criteria: All ten corrected; each labelled with the right pattern; numbers 7 and 8 corrected in opposite directions; numbers 9 and 10 fix structure rather than grammar
writing.support: Numbers 7 and 8 are the same four words meaning opposite things, and the only signal is the form of the verb. Write both out with their meanings beside them before correcting either.
writing.extension: Numbers 9 and 10 were both perfectly correct English that failed anyway. Write one more of each kind.

activities.title: Practice 1 — Which preposition, which form?
activities.instructions:
Write the preposition, and the correct form of any verb in brackets.
1. I am interested ____ (work) here.
2. She is capable ____ (do) far more.
3. I was worried ____ the delay.
4. He is good ____ (explain) things.
5. I am proud ____ (finish) it.
6. She was disappointed ____ the answer.
7. I am not keen ____ the new arrangement.
8. I was not aware ____ the change.
9. I am tired ____ (explain) it.
10. She is involved ____ the project.
11. He was annoyed ____ the delay.
12. I am afraid ____ (get) it wrong.
13. She is satisfied ____ the result.
14. I am ashamed ____ (not ask) sooner.
15. He is hopeless ____ (remember) names.
16. They were excited ____ the change.
activities.answers:
1. in working  2. of doing  3. about  4. at explaining  5. of finishing  6. with  7. on  8. of  9. of explaining  10. in  11. about  12. of getting  13. with  14. of not asking  15. at remembering  16. about
Every verb in the list came out as an -ing form. That rule has no exceptions and it is worth checking all eight before anything else.
The tendencies held for most: of in 2, 5, 8, 9, 12 and 14; about in 3, 11 and 16; with in 6 and 13; at in 4 and 15; in in 1 and 10.
Number 7 is the exception. Keen takes on for a thing and to for an action, and no tendency predicts it.

activities.title: Practice 2 — Used to, be used to, or past simple?
activities.instructions:
Choose the right form.
1. I (used to work / am used to working) nights, but I stopped in 2019.
2. I (used to work / am used to working) nights now — I have adapted.
3. I (used to work / worked) nights for two years. (a plain fact about a period)
4. (Did you use to / Did you used to) work nights?
5. I (didn't use to / didn't used to) like it.
6. She (used to live / is used to living) abroad, but she came back.
7. He (is used to / used to) getting up early — he has done it for years.
8. We (used to have / are used to having) a shop on this street.
9. I (didn't use to / am not used to) working in an office.  (I have not adapted)
10. They (used to be / are used to being) much stricter about it.
11. I (used to smoke / am used to smoking), but not any more.
12. She (is used to / used to) the noise now.
activities.answers:
1. used to work  2. am used to working  3. worked  4. Did you use to  5. didn't use to  6. used to live  7. is used to  8. used to have  9. am not used to  10. used to be  11. used to smoke  12. is used to
Numbers 4 and 5 both have did, so used loses its d. In speech there is no difference; in writing there is.
Numbers 2, 7, 9 and 12 are all be used to — an adaptation, present and continuing. Every one is followed by -ing or a noun.
Number 3 is the plain past simple, because it states a fact about a period with no implication that a habit stopped. If you chose used to there it would also be correct English, but it would be saying something slightly different.

activities.title: Practice 3 — From list to narrative
activities.instructions:
Here is a list of facts about one person.
· Left school at 17
· Worked in a bakery for two years
· Moved cities in 2016
· Worked in three different call centres over four years
· In 2020 volunteered to train new staff, unpaid
· Found she was good at it
· Trained about forty people over two years
· Now applying for a teaching course
Rewrite this as four paragraphs using compress, mark, expand, look back.
Every fact must survive, but not every fact deserves a sentence.
activities.answers:
Model answer — yours will differ.
I left school at seventeen and spent the next six years in work I did not choose: two years in a bakery, then three call centres in four years after I moved cities in 2016.
In 2020 I volunteered to train the new intake. Nobody asked me to and it was unpaid.
I expected to dislike it. Instead it was the first work I had ever been reluctant to stop doing at the end of the day. I trained about forty people over the following two years, and I got better at it in a way I could actually notice — the fourth group understood things in an afternoon that the first group had taken a week over. I started staying late to rewrite the material, which nobody had asked for and nobody objected to.
At the time I thought of it as something I did alongside my job. Looking back, it was the only part of six years of work that I would want to do again, which is why I am applying.
Check three things in yours. Are all eight facts present? Is the compression paragraph shorter than the expansion by a clear margin? And do the last two sentences disagree with each other?
The fact that deserves the most space is volunteered to train new staff, because it is the turning point. The bakery deserves five words.

activities.title: Practice 4 — At the time, looking back
activities.instructions:
Write ten sentences — five pairs.
For each pair, write what you thought at the time and what you think looking back.
Use a different opening for each: at the time, I remember thinking, it seemed, I assumed, I was convinced.
And for the second half: looking back, reflecting on it now, with hindsight, I appreciate now, I realise now.
Each pair must disagree with itself.
activities.answers:
No key for the content — they are your events. But check three things.
First, does each pair disagree? If the at-the-time view and the looking-back view are the same, the second sentence is doing no work and the pair should be rewritten.
Second, did you use ten different openings? Repeating looking back five times is the commonest result and it flattens the effect.
Third, and this is the useful one: how many of your pairs move from negative to positive? Most people write five of those, because the reinterpretation that comes easily is the one where something bad turns out well. Try writing one that goes the other way — something you were pleased about at the time and see differently now. It is harder and it is more interesting.

activities.title: Practice 5 — Collect twenty pairs
activities.instructions:
This week, collect twenty adjective-and-preposition pairs from real English — anything you read or hear.
Write each one down inside the phrase you found it in, not on its own.
Then sort them by preposition and see which tendencies held.
Mark any that contradict the tendencies on card 1.
activities.answers:
No key — they are your pairs.
What most people find: of dominates, as the card says, and the sorting confirms it within about fifteen examples. About and with together account for most of the rest.
The second finding is more useful. The contradictions you collect are the pairs worth memorising, because a pair that follows a tendency can be guessed and one that does not cannot. Most people find between two and four contradictions in twenty, and those four are worth more attention than the other sixteen combined.
Writing them inside a phrase rather than alone matters. A pair learned as good at is two words; a pair learned as she's very good at explaining things is a sentence you can reuse.

activities.title: Practice 6 — Tell it to somebody
activities.instructions:
This week, tell four minutes of your story to one real person, using the shape.
Do not tell them you are doing an exercise.
Afterwards, write three lines: where they asked a question, where they looked lost, and whether they understood which part you were building towards.
If you cannot do this with a person, record it and leave it a week, then listen as a stranger.
activities.answers:
No key.
What most people find: the questions come at the seam between compression and expansion, because the compressed part raises questions the expansion does not answer. That is usually a sign the compression is doing its job — the listener is interested in something you deliberately skipped, and you can answer in one sentence.
The second finding is about the mark. If your listener could not say afterwards which part you were building towards, the marking sentence was either missing or too long. A mark that works is short, and its shortness is what makes it audible.

options: I am interested in to work here.
I am interested in working here.
I am interested to working here.
I am interested on working here.
quizzes.a: I am interested in working here.
quizzes.why: Interested takes in, and whatever follows a preposition is a noun or an -ing form — never a plain verb. That second rule has no exceptions.

quizzes.q: If you are stuck and must guess a preposition, which is the best guess?
quizzes.why: It is the commonest by a wide margin — aware of, capable of, proud of, afraid of, tired of. The tendencies are for guessing under pressure, not for construction.

options: He is good in explaining things.
He is good of explaining things.
He is good at explain things.
He is good at explaining things.
quizzes.a: He is good at explaining things.
quizzes.why: At attaches to ability, and the verb after the preposition takes -ing.

quizzes.q: I used to work nights. What does your listener understand?
options: That you no longer work nights
That you have adapted to nights
quizzes.a: That you no longer work nights
quizzes.why: The implication that the habit has stopped is not optional — it is the whole point of the form, and it is heard without being said.

options: I didn't used to like it.
I didn't use to like it.
I not used to like it.
quizzes.a: I didn't use to like it.
quizzes.why: When did appears, used loses its d. You hear no difference at all in speech, which is why the written error survives so long.

quizzes.q: I'm used to working nights. What does it mean?
options: I did them once and stopped
I have adapted, and probably still do them
I am about to start them
quizzes.a: I have adapted, and probably still do them
quizzes.why: Be used to plus -ing is an adaptation. Used to plus a plain verb is a stopped habit. The only signal is the form of the verb.

quizzes.q: What is the difference between I worked nights for two years and I used to work nights?
options: The second means you still do
The first is a fact about a period; the second says it was a habit that stopped
quizzes.a: The first is a fact about a period; the second says it was a habit that stopped
quizzes.why: Both are correct and they say different things. The past simple states; used to implies a change.

quizzes.q: What are the three moves of a life story in English?
quizzes.why: Detail goes only after a mark. Giving equal detail to everything produces a timetable, and the listener cannot tell what you are building towards.

quizzes.q: Reading 2 says compression is not a failure to give detail. Why not?
options: Because covering a decade in eight words signals that nothing there needs detail
quizzes.a: Because covering a decade in eight words signals that nothing there needs detail
quizzes.why: Compression communicates something. Learners often feel skipping years is dishonest, when it is the move that directs attention.

quizzes.q: What does a looking-back sentence do that the other three moves cannot?
options: It tells the listener what to make of an event
quizzes.a: It tells the listener what to make of an event
quizzes.why: Without it the listener has to guess whether an event was good or bad news. It also makes an account sound reflective rather than chronological.

quizzes.q: Version A of the personal statement is entirely correct English. Why does it fail?
options: It is a timetable — nothing is marked as important
quizzes.a: It is a timetable — nothing is marked as important
quizzes.why: Every period gets equal weight and the reader learns no more from the eighth sentence than from the first. The failure is structural, not linguistic.

quizzes.q: Why do Version B's adjective-and-preposition claims work better than Version A's?
options: They are attached to evidence the reader has already been given
They are in the first paragraph
quizzes.a: They are attached to evidence the reader has already been given
quizzes.why: The grammar is identical in both. A's could describe anybody; B's capable of catching up is a conclusion the reader has grounds for.

teacherNotes.note: Three pattern cards, each with a worked example, and every exercise has an answer key or an explicit no-key note with a what-most-people-find finding. Practice 2 is the diagnostic and it deliberately mixes three forms — used to, be used to and the plain past simple — because the confusion is three-way rather than two-way. Practices 5 and 6 are field tasks with no key.

teacherNotes.type: Card 1 admits there is no rule, and should
teacherNotes.note: Learners spend real time searching for a system behind adjective and preposition pairings. Saying plainly that there is none, and then offering tendencies as a guessing strategy rather than as rules, is more honest and more useful. The one thing on the card that never fails — a noun or -ing form after the preposition — is flagged as such, and it is the error worth fixing first because it is mechanical.

Used to plus a plain verb, be used to plus -ing, and the plain past simple describe three different situations, and the first two are four identical words apart. Writing 4 numbers 7 and 8 are that pair deliberately adjacent and corrected in opposite directions. The didn't used to spelling error is invisible in speech, which is why it survives into advanced writing and why the card says so explicitly.

teacherNotes.type: Card 3 is structure, not grammar, and it carries the unit
teacherNotes.note: Compress, mark, expand, look back is the difference between Version A and Version B in Reading 3, and neither version contains a grammatical error. Learners default to chronological equal-weight accounts and run out of time before the point. The half-your-time-on-one-thing test is deliberately crude because it is checkable — Speaking 4 asks learners to time their own expansion.

teacherNotes.type: Why two versions of one life
teacherNotes.note: Version A is entirely correct English and entirely uninformative, which makes the failure visible as structure rather than as language. Four of the ten comprehension questions turn on that distinction. The last two sentences of Version B are the strongest demonstration of the looking-back move available: placed at the end, they recast three paragraphs the reader has already accepted.

teacherNotes.type: The at-the-time and looking-back pair must disagree
teacherNotes.note: This is the criterion learners most often miss. A pair where both halves say the same thing is doing no work, and Practice 4's key asks a further question worth raising: almost everybody writes reinterpretations that move from negative to positive, because that is the easy direction. Asking for one that goes the other way produces noticeably more interesting writing.

The AI tutor is a rehearsal partner and no task here is scored by it alone. This unit asks learners to write and record their own life story at length — Writing 1, Speaking 4 and Practice 6 all involve genuinely personal material, potentially including difficult periods. None of it should be collected, shared or entered into the app, and learners choose what to include. Practice 6 asks learners to tell their story to a real person and to record only where questions were asked and where the listener looked lost — not the content of what they said, and not the other person's response. That wording should stay.

selfAssessment.statement: I can say interested in working here and good at explaining things without hesitating.
I can say I used to work nights and be understood to mean I no longer do.
I can tell my own story so that the important parts stand out.
I can read a personal statement and say what makes it work or fail.

assignment.title: A life told twice
assignment.instructions: Two parts. First, record four minutes of your own story using compress, mark, expand and look back, spending at least half the time on one thing, with at least four adjective-and-preposition pairs and two used-to sentences — then listen twice, time your expansion, and record one further sentence saying whether it reached half. Second, write the four-paragraph version from Writing 1, then rewrite Version A from Reading 3 as directed in Writing 2, keeping every date and job, with the four lines of commentary. Add your full-sentence answers to the five questions in Writing 3. Keep everything together.
